content.intro: This lesson focuses on deploying backend applications. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Deploying Backend Applications matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Backend deployment needs a reproducible deployable package, protected credentials, target-specific config, and post-deploy health checks. Deployment workflows should promote a known artifact through controlled environments, restrict credentials and concurrency, verify health, and define rollback conditions before production use.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Backend deployment needs a reproducible deployable package, protected credentials, target-specific config, and post-deploy health checks. Deployment workflows should promote a known artifact through controlled environments, restrict credentials and concurrency, verify health, and define rollback conditions before production use. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Building deployable application packages
items.text: Trace the release to a source commit, validate the selected version/ref, restrict publication permissions, retain build evidence, and verify the published artifact before promoting it.

items.title: Preparing deployment credentials
items.text: Store credentials in the appropriate protected secret store, pass them only to the step that needs them, and never print or save them in logs, summaries, artifacts, or caches.

items.title: Configuring hosting targets
items.text: For configuring hosting targets, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Deploying APIs and backend services
items.text: Use a scoped token, validate request inputs and event payloads, check HTTP/error status, handle pagination and rate limits, and avoid logging credentials or unneeded private response data.

items.title: Health checks after deployment
items.text: For health checks after deployment, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Environment-specific configuration
items.text: Use a GitHub Environment for deployment-specific secrets, variables, branch restrictions, and reviewer gates. Do not treat an environment name alone as proof that approval rules are configured.

items.title: Handling deployment failures
items.text: Start with the first failed step and its exit code, then inspect the event, conditions, permissions, tool versions, network, and runner state. Capture sanitized diagnostics and preserve evidence of the failure.

content_blocks.code:
jobs:
  deploy-staging:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - run: echo "Verify known artifact before deploy"
content_blocks.expected_output: The job is associated with the staging environment and read-only repository access; actual deployment credentials and environment protections must be configured separately.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository or static validation first. Confirm the snippet matches the repository, runner, permissions, and current GitHub documentation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove temporary test workflows and never carry test credentials or sample outputs into production.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to deploying backend applications. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain deploying backend applications, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Move known build outputs through controlled environments with auditable approvals and recovery plans.

content.task: Apply deploying backend applications to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Backend deployment needs a reproducible deployable package, protected credentials, target-specific config, and post-deploy health checks.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Backend deployment needs a reproducible deployable package, protected credentials, target-specific config, and post-deploy health checks. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Backend deployment needs a reproducible deployable package, protected credentials, target-specific config, and post-deploy health checks.
Deployment workflows should promote a known artifact through controlled environments, restrict credentials and concurrency, verify health, and define rollback conditions before production use.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
